source.title: Unleashing the Potential of Sparse Attention on Long-term Behaviors for CTR Prediction
source.authors: Weijiang Lai; Beihong Jin; Di Zhang; Si-Ru Chen; Jiongyan Zhang; Yuhang Gou; Jian Dong; Xing-Xing Wang

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling in the new setting of CTR recommendation models, using AUC rather than the language-model pretraining loss used in the original claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports fitted AUC-versus-FLOPs curves for four SparseCTR scales. It does not report held-out cross-entropy loss, a small-run-to-large-run prediction test, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.test_reason: Section 4.6 fits a saturating power law, AUC(X) = E − A/X^α, to AUC against FLOPs for four SparseCTR scales on an industrial CTR dataset. That is a scaling result in a new setting: recommendation, with AUC as the measure. The paper is mainly a method paper, but this section reports its own scaling measurements, so it bears on V5. It does not test V1–V4, V6 or V7 for language models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SparseCTR shows an obvious scaling-law phenomenon, with AUC rising with FLOPs over three orders of magnitude. They also claim that jointly increasing sequence length and model scale is more efficient than increasing either alone, but they state this as an insight from the fits without a dedicated test.
record.recipe_differences: Fits AUC, not held-out language-model loss, against FLOPs in a CTR recommender system; FLOPs vary through both model scale and sequence length. The study does not fit loss against parameters, tokens, or compute separately.
record.method_sensitivity: The FLOPs sweep varies both model scale and sequence length; the study does not isolate their separate effects.
record.problems: The scaling analysis is limited to one CTR dataset and AUC rather than held-out loss. The plotted fits are reported, but the underlying AUC points and their uncertainty are not provided in the text.

untested.parts: Held-out loss (the study measures AUC, not cross-entropy). Data/token scaling, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, image or video. No single power law fitted across all scales. No extrapolation test.
All. The claim that jointly scaling sequence length and model size is more efficient is asserted, not shown as a compute-optimal analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The fitted asymptote E = 0.73 is identical for all four scales, possibly constrained or shared; the text does not say. The three-orders-of-magnitude span requires pooling across scales, while each fitted curve covers about one order. The study is not an original source. This is evidence from a small-model recommendation domain, peripheral to the language-model claim.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No test of predictions from fits on smaller runs against larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests AUC scaling in CTR recommendation, not cross-entropy loss; it does not test other modalities or the listed training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task evaluation of language models or relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance.
Does not compare fitting choices or setups to test whether exponents or compute-optimal allocations change, and does not test curve bending.

rows.subject: SparseCTR Scale-1
rows.operation_detail: Fits AUC as a power-law function of FLOPs using sequence lengths 128, 256, 512, and 1024.
rows.measure: Fitted AUC(X) versus FLOPs curve; R²
rows.note: The figure gives the fitted equation and R²; the text says the fits indicate that AUC increases with computational cost.
rows.check: FLOPs within this scale vary only through sequence length (128–1024, about 8x), giving about 4 points per fit. The 3-parameter fit (E, A, α) on about 4 points makes R² near 1 weak evidence. The underlying AUC points can only be read from the figure.

rows.subject: SparseCTR Scale-2
rows.operation_detail: Fits AUC as a power-law function of FLOPs using sequence lengths 128, 256, 512, and 1024.
rows.measure: Fitted AUC(X) versus FLOPs curve; R²
rows.note: The figure gives the fitted equation and R²; the text says the fits indicate that AUC increases with computational cost.
rows.check: Same as R1: about 4 points per curve, and FLOPs vary only through sequence length within the scale.

rows.subject: SparseCTR Scale-4
rows.operation_detail: Fits AUC as a power-law function of FLOPs using sequence lengths 128, 256, 512, and 1024.

rows.check: Same as R1. The three-orders-of-magnitude FLOPs span comes only from pooling across all four scales; no single curve fitted over the full range is reported.

relationships.condition: SparseCTR CTR models, 35K–2.7M non-embedding parameters, Industry dataset, FLOPs varied by sequence length within each scale
relationships.reason: Per-scale power-law fits of AUC against FLOPs give R² of 0.994–0.998, with AUC rising with FLOPs (R1–R4). This is weak evidence: about 4 points per 3-parameter fit, AUC rather than loss, and one dataset.
relationships.display_finding: AUC increased with FLOPs, with power-law R² values of 0.994–0.998, although each three-parameter fit used approximately four points from one dataset.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SparseCTR on the Industry dataset, across the four reported model scales and sequence lengths
reader_labels.reason: The reported AUC-versus-FLOPs fits have R² values from 0.994 to 0.998, and the authors describe increasing AUC with increased computational cost (R1–R4). This supports a power-law-like scaling result in this CTR setting, not the claimed language-model loss result.
